Photograph: Rahat Dar/EPA Rights and freedom Pakistan Pakistan precinct suspends all 78 officers and staff over alleged rape at police station Lahore police official says all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing at station Supported by About this content Haroon Janjua in Islamabad Wed 5 Aug 2026 11.23 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The alleged rape of a 20-year-old woman with learning disabilities in a police station in Lahore, Pakistan , has prompted authorities to suspend all 78 police officers and staff at the precinct, in one of the country’s biggest ever disciplinary actions against its police force. The woman alleges that an assistant sub-inspector apprehended her, took her to Ghaziabad police station and raped her in a room on the second floor. The woman’s family said she disappeared on the street, before returning home in tears and stating that she had been sexually assaulted at the station. The accused officer has been arrested and is now facing a criminal investigation for rape. All 78 police officials and staff members of Lahore’s Ghaziabad police station were suspended on Tuesday. Lahore’s deputy inspector general of police (operations), Faisal Kamran, told the Guardian that the officers were suspended because, under police rules, all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing within the station and they had failed to do so. “No officer questioned why the assistant sub-inspector had brought the woman to the station without any female police personnel present,” Kamran said. “I suspended all 78 police officials, and the gender crime wing is investigating the case, and we will dismiss the culprits, and we will ensure the safety of all police stations in the city,” he added. The case has sparked outrage in Pakistan, where rights groups have long claimed many women are reluctant to report sexual violence because of stigma and a lack of confidence in law enforcement. Allegations of misconduct by police officers have further eroded public trust, activists say. “This is an extremely disturbing incident and reflects the longstanding lack of accountability within the police,” said Farzana Bari, a women’s rights activist. “It is a stark example of the abuse of power. Allegations of police misconduct and custodial rape are not new, and we have seen such cases over the years. “We campaigned relentlessly in the 1990s for women’s police stations because survivors often did not feel safe reporting abuse to male officers. While the police’s record on protecting women remains poor, the fact that this case has been reported offers some hope that justice will be served.” Convictions for rape remain rare despite legal reforms in recent years. The Sustainable Social Development Organisation said the national conviction rate was about 0.5% in 2024, while official data showed the rate in Punjab, where the incident occurred, was 4% in 2025. Rights groups attribute the low rates to weak investigations, poor evidence collection, delays in prosecutions and the stigma surrounding sexual violence. According to police data , there were more than 20,000 crimes against women in Punjab province in the first half of 2026, up from the same period in 2025. “Unless state institutions are held accountable, such crimes will continue. What is needed is structural reform and stronger oversight to ensure justice for ordinary people,” Bari said. Text Groups eNewsletter Facebook Twitter Instagram Pinterest Youtube Soundcloud Faith Request Prayer Thought For The Day Our Catholic Faith Rosary Traditional Prayers Confession Find a Mass Daily Readings Catholic News Diocese of Saint Petersburg Listen Live Spirit FM 90.5 (HD1) The Light (HD2) El Fuego (HD3) Give Now Catholic News Vandals deface Our Lady statues, set fire to altar at Medjugorje shrine http://www.myspiritfm.com/News?blogid=Catholic-News&view=post&articleid=301923&link=1&fldKeywords=&fldAuthor=&fldTopic=0 The parish called on the faithful to respond "with prayer, fasting, and forgiveness" as police arrested a suspect and cleanup began days before the Mladifest youth festival. Vandals desecrated two statues of Our Lady and set fire to the outdoor altar of St. James Church at the Medjugorje shrine in Bosnia and Herzegovina early Tuesday, July 28, days before the shrine's annual Mladifest youth festival. The statue of Our Lady on Podbrdo, or Apparition Hill, was doused with black paint across the face, chest, and dress, with the words "Devil in a skirt" scrawled on its pedestal, local media reported . The statue of Our Lady at the nearby Blue Cross was similarly defaced, with "EVIL" written on a nearby stone slab. A banner in Polish naming the six alleged seers was left near the Podbrdo statue . Police in Citluk received the first report at 4:30 a.m. and a report of fire at the recently renovated altar behind St. James parish church at 5 a.m., a police spokeswoman said reportedly. Surveillance footage shows a man dousing the altar with flammable liquid and igniting it. Cantonal police later confirmed to local media that a suspect was arrested Tuesday afternoon. His identity has not been released. 'Prayer, fasting, and forgiveness' "We received with great sadness the news of the act of vandalism that damaged the places of prayer in our parish," the Medjugorje parish office said in a statement , calling on the faithful to respond "as Our Lady has been teaching us in Medjugorje for more than 40 years: with prayer, fasting, and forgiveness." Cleanup began immediately, the parish said, and "the shrine remains open to all pilgrims." Bishop Petar Palic of Mostar-Duvno expressed deep sorrow, urging the faithful not to let evil "infect us with its own logic," while the Interreligious Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina condemned the attack. The Vatican granted a "nihil obstat" to devotion at Medjugorje in September 2024. Mladifest opens Aug. 1 and is expected to draw 50,000 to 60,000 pilgrims. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/20/iran.text: Iran has positioned more than 14 oil tankers at Kharg Island in a convoy poised to attempt to break the US naval blockade of its oil exports, satellite imagery and ship-tracking data show.Crews have been assigned to the tankers, Iranian flags have been raised over them, and Tehran plans to send them in convoy toward the Sea of Oman exit in the coming days, the reports said.Ship-tracking firm TankerTrackers said available data confirmed Iran was resuming oil exports.International media outlets reported on Thursday that an Iranian crude cargo had already been transferred between two tankers in a ship-to-ship operation in the Persian Gulf as the blockade tightened.Satellite imagery and shipping data showed the transfers took place near Kharg Island with automatic identification systems (AIS) switched off to conceal the oil's origin. Washington had previously warned it would target vessels involved in such operations.Israel's Channel 14 and Sabereen News, an outlet close to Iran-backed armed groups, reported that dozens of Iranian tankers were preparing to head towards China and were moving closer to the blockade lines.A journalist with ties to Iran's IRGC threatened publicly that any attack on the tankers would lead to strikes on oil facilities across the Gulf.Mohammad Enayati Najafabadi, in a post on X resharing a piece by Iran's state-affiliated Fars news agency, warned that disrupting an Iranian tanker's route "will lead to explosions at the oil facilities of the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain," which he described as a personal analysis.The Fars piece used an image from the Shahnameh, the Persian epic, depicting the mythical hero Fereydoun defending Iranian ships at sea — a reference its authors explicitly drew to the US blockade.Kharg Island remains crucialKharg Island, in the northern Persian Gulf, accounts for around 85% to 90% of Iran's crude oil exports.Its terminal can store around 30 million barrels and has waters deep enough to berth supertankers. The halt to loading operations since the naval blockade was imposed has placed mounting financial pressure on Tehran.Alternative terminals including the port of Jask lack the infrastructure to replace it.Tehran's moves come as Trump, during a recent visit to China where he met Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, signalled no urgency over Iran and indicated the issue would not be addressed until next year.Iranian authorities appear to be using that window to restore oil exports to Asian markets and ease pressure on state finances.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, speaking on Fox News on Thursday, said energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz were increasing despite the tensions.Asked why petrol prices in the US had fallen even as the Iran standoff appeared unresolved, Wright said conditions had in fact changed but were not yet visible to the public.The US had been moving more oil through the Strait of Hormuz and exporting more refined products — petrol, diesel and jet fuel — for several weeks, he said, claiming supply had actually risen.
